rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Predict the reagent for carrying out the following transformations : (Any two)
(i) Benzoyl chloride to Benzaldehyde
(ii) Ethanal to 3-hydroxy butanal
(iii) Ethanoic acid to 2-chloroethanoic acid
rows.solution:
(i) BENZOYL CHLORIDE TO BENZALDEHYDE — hydrogen over PALLADIUM ON BARIUM SULPHATE, the ROSENMUND REDUCTION:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd}/\mathrm{BaSO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The catalyst is deliberately POISONED, with sulphur or quinoline and by the inert support, so that it is not active enough to reduce the aldehyde on to benzyl alcohol. Stopping at the right stage is the whole point.

(ii) ETHANAL TO 3-HYDROXYBUTANAL — DILUTE ALKALI, an ALDOL ADDITION:
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}\)

Count the carbons: TWO in, FOUR out, so two molecules are joined. Note the product is the ALDOL itself, not the condensation product — so the mixture must be kept COLD. Warming it would eliminate water and give but-2-enal.

(iii) ETHANOIC ACID TO 2-CHLOROETHANOIC ACID — CHLORINE with a little RED PHOSPHORUS, the HELL-VOLHARD-ZELINSKY reaction:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}\)

The phosphorus is essential: it converts the acid into its acyl chloride, which enolises far more readily than the acid, and it is the enol that chlorine attacks.

rows.subtopic: Conductance of Electrolytic Solutions
rows.stem:
(i) Why on dilution the \(\Lambda_m\) of \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) increases very fast, while that of \(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\) increases gradually ?
(ii) What happens if external potential applied becomes greater than \(\mathrm{E^\circ}\) cell of electrochemical cell ?
rows.solution:
(i) Because they are different KINDS of electrolyte, and the two rises have different causes.

ACETIC ACID is a WEAK electrolyte, only slightly ionised. Diluting shifts its ionisation equilibrium towards MORE ions, so one mole of acid furnishes many more of them — the degree of dissociation itself is changing, and the molar conductivity rises very steeply, most steeply of all near infinite dilution.

SODIUM ACETATE is a STRONG electrolyte, completely dissociated at every concentration. No new ions can appear, so the only thing dilution changes is how much the existing ions interfere with one another's migration — and that is a small effect, giving a gradual rise.

The difference shows on a graph: sodium acetate gives a near straight line against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) that can be extrapolated to \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\); acetic acid gives a curve that never meets the axis, so its limiting value must come from Kohlrausch's law.

(ii) The reaction REVERSES and the cell becomes an ELECTROLYTIC cell.

While the external potential is LESS than \(E_{\text{cell}}\), the cell drives current in the usual direction and the spontaneous reaction proceeds. When the two are EQUAL, no current flows and the reaction stops — this is the null point used to measure emf.

Once the external potential EXCEEDS \(E_{\text{cell}}\), current is forced through in the OPPOSITE direction and every electrode reaction runs backwards. In a Daniell cell, zinc is now deposited at the zinc electrode and copper dissolves, so the cell is being CHARGED rather than discharged — which is exactly what happens when a lead storage battery is recharged.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Amines
rows.stem: An Organic compound (A) with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_7NO}\) on heating with \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) and KOH forms a compound (B). Compound (B) on heating with \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and alcoholic KOH produces a foul smelling compound (C) and on reacting with \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\) forms a compound (D) which is soluble in alkali. Write the structures of (A), (B), (C) and (D).
rows.solution:
Work through the clues in order.

Compound (B) gives a FOUL SMELLING product with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide — that is the CARBYLAMINE reaction, and it works only for a PRIMARY amine. The test with benzenesulphonyl chloride confirms it: the product (D) DISSOLVES IN ALKALI, which in Hinsberg's test marks a primary amine.

So (B) is a primary amine, and (A) — molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_7NO}\), heated with bromine and alkali — must be the AMIDE that Hofmann degradation converts into it, with the loss of ONE carbon:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CONH_2}\), propanamide
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethanamine

The two remaining products follow:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NC}\), ethyl isocyanide — the foul smelling compound
\(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2NHC_2H_5}\), N-ethylbenzenesulphonamide

(D) dissolves in alkali because its remaining \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen is made ACIDIC by the two strongly electron-withdrawing sulphonyl oxygens. A secondary amine's sulphonamide has no such hydrogen and stays insoluble, which is what makes the test discriminating.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) salts are coloured while \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) salts are white.
(ii) \(\mathrm{E^\circ}\) value for the \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}\) couple is much more positive than that for \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\).
(iii) Transition metals form alloys.
rows.solution:
(i) Because \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) has a PARTLY FILLED d subshell and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) has a FULL one.

Colour arises from a D-D TRANSITION: a ligand field splits the five d orbitals into two sets, and an electron absorbs visible light to jump from the lower set to the upper. The jump needs an ELECTRON below and a VACANCY above.

Copper(II) is \(3d^9\) — one unpaired electron and a vacancy available — so its salts are blue. Zinc(II) is \(3d^{10}\), completely full, with nowhere to jump, so its salts are white.

(ii) Because reducing \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) REACHES a stable configuration while reducing \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) DESTROYS one.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is \(3d^4\), and gaining one electron gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled subshell. The change is strongly favoured, so \(E^{\circ}\) is large and positive, \(+1{\cdot}57\) V.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) is \(3d^3\), which in an octahedral aqueous environment is the stable HALF-FILLED \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Reducing it to \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) would break that up, so the change is unfavourable and \(E^{\circ}\) is negative, \(-0{\cdot}41\) V.

The third ionisation energy of manganese is also much larger than chromium's, which says the same thing from the other side.

(iii) Because their ATOMIC RADII are very similar.

Across the transition series the radii differ by only a few picometres, so one metal's atoms can replace another's in the crystal lattice without disturbing the structure. Such a SUBSTITUTIONAL alloy forms readily, and its properties — hardness, corrosion resistance — often exceed those of either component. Brass, bronze and stainless steel are the familiar examples.

rows.subtopic: Nernst Equation
rows.stem:
Calculate \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) and log Kc for the following cell :
\(\mathrm{Ni(s) + 2\,Ag^+(aq) \rightarrow Ni^{2+}(aq) + 2Ag(s)}\)
Given that \(\mathrm{E^\circ}\)cell = 1.05V, IF = 96,500 \(\mathrm{Cmol^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
The standard free energy change follows from the cell potential. The reaction \(\mathrm{Ni} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\) transfers TWO electrons, so \(n = 2\):
\(\Delta_r \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n\mathrm{F}E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -2 \times 96500 \times 1{\cdot}05\)

\(\Delta_r \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -202650\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(-202{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The equilibrium constant comes from the same potential, through the relation that holds when the cell has run down to equilibrium and its emf has fallen to zero:
\(\log \mathrm{K_C} = \dfrac{n\,E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}}{0{\cdot}059} = \dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}05}{0{\cdot}059}\)

\(\log \mathrm{K_C} = 35{\cdot}6\)

The two answers agree in what they say. A large NEGATIVE free energy change and an enormous equilibrium constant — \(\mathrm{K_C}\) around \(10^{35{\cdot}6}\) — both mean the same thing: the reaction goes essentially to completion.

rows.subtopic: Nernst Equation
rows.stem:
Calculate the e.m.f. of the following cell at 298K :
\(\mathrm{Fe(s)\,|\,Fe^{2+}\,(0.001\ M)\,||\,H^{+}\,(0.01M)\,|\,H_2(g)\,(1\ bar)\,|\,Pt(s)}\)
Given that \(\mathrm{E^\circ}\)cell = +0.44 V
[log 2 = 0.3010   log 3 = 0.4771   log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
Read the cell diagram: iron is on the LEFT and so is the anode, oxidised to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\); hydrogen ions are reduced at the right.

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Fe} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid iron does not enter the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}44 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}001}{(0{\cdot}01)^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}44 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-4}} = 0{\cdot}44 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log 10\)
\(= 0{\cdot}44 - 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}4105\ \mathrm{V}\)

The SQUARED term is where marks are lost: \((0{\cdot}01)^2\) is \(10^{-4}\), so the quotient is 10 and not \(10^{-1}\). The hydrogen ion's coefficient of 2 carries through as an exponent.

rows.subtopic: Bonding in Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
(a) Using valence bond theory, predict the hybridization and magnetic character of following :
\(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) [Atomic number of Co = 27]
(b) Write IUPAC name of the following complex :
\(\mathrm{[CoBr_2(en)_2]^{+}}\)
(c) How many ions are produced from the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_2}\) in solution ?
rows.solution:
(a) Cobalt is atomic number 27, and six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so cobalt is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\).

FLUORIDE is a WEAK field ligand. It cannot force the six electrons to pair up, so they spread out as far as Hund's rule allows — one pair and FOUR UNPAIRED electrons — and no inner \(3d\) orbital is left free.

Bonding must therefore reach OUTWARDS to the \(4d\) set, giving \(sp^3d^2\) hybridisation and an OCTAHEDRAL shape. This is an OUTER ORBITAL or high spin complex, and it is PARAMAGNETIC, \(\mu = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = 4{\cdot}90\) B.M.

The contrast with \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is the lesson: the same ion with a strong field ligand pairs all six electrons, becomes \(d^2sp^3\) and is diamagnetic.

(b) The two bromido ligands give \(-2\) and the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral, so against an overall \(+1\) cobalt must be \(+3\). The chelating ligand's name already contains a multiplying prefix, so it takes BIS and brackets:
DIBROMIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)COBALT(III) ION

(c) THREE ions.

Only what sits OUTSIDE the square brackets ionises. The six ammines are ligands and stay with the cobalt; the two chlorides are counter ions:
\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-}\)

One complex cation plus two chloride ions — three in all, which is exactly what a conductivity measurement reports.

rows.subtopic: Colloids
rows.stem:
Differentiate between the following :
(i) Adsorption and Absorption
(ii) Lyophobic Sol and Lyophilic Sol
(iii) Multimolecular Colloid and Macromolecular colloid.
rows.solution:
(i) ADSORPTION is the accumulation of a substance at the SURFACE of a solid or liquid, so the concentration is higher at the surface than in the bulk. ABSORPTION is uniform distribution THROUGHOUT the bulk of the material.

Silica gel ADSORBS water vapour on its surface; anhydrous calcium chloride ABSORBS it into its mass. Adsorption is also rapid and reaches equilibrium quickly, while absorption is slow and steady.

(ii) A LYOPHOBIC sol is "solvent repelling" — irreversible, unstable, easily coagulated by a trace of electrolyte, and needing special methods of preparation. A LYOPHILIC sol is "solvent loving" — reversible, stable, difficult to coagulate, and forming on simple mixing.

(iii) A MULTIMOLECULAR colloid is an AGGREGATE of a large number of small molecules or atoms, which together fall in the colloidal size range; the particles are held by weak van der Waals forces. A gold sol and a sulphur sol are examples.

A MACROMOLECULAR colloid has particles that are SINGLE LARGE MOLECULES, each already of colloidal size. Starch, proteins and polythene give such sols, and they are generally lyophilic and stable.

rows.subtopic: Colloids
rows.stem:
(I) Define the following terms :
(i) Zeta Potential
(ii) Coagulation
(II) Why a negatively charged sol is obtained when \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution is added to KI solution ?
rows.solution:
(I)(i) ZETA POTENTIAL is the potential difference between the FIXED LAYER of ions adsorbed on the surface of a colloidal particle and the DIFFUSE LAYER of oppositely charged ions spread through the medium around it.

It is also called the electrokinetic potential, and it is what makes the particles repel one another. A sol is stable so long as the zeta potential is large enough; reducing it, by adding an electrolyte, lets the particles approach and coagulate.

(ii) COAGULATION is the settling of colloidal particles — the conversion of a sol into a PRECIPITATE. It happens when the charge on the particles is neutralised so that they can no longer repel one another, and they then collide and grow heavy enough to fall out. Adding an electrolyte is the usual way; boiling, persistent dialysis and mixing two oppositely charged sols do the same.

(II) Because the silver iodide particles adsorb IODIDE ions from the excess potassium iodide.

Adding silver nitrate TO potassium iodide leaves the IODIDE in excess, and a precipitate preferentially adsorbs the ion it has in COMMON with the surrounding solution. The particles therefore take up \(\mathrm{I^-}\) and acquire a negative charge:
\(\mathrm{AgI}/\mathrm{I^-}\) — a negatively charged sol

Reversing the order of addition reverses the sign. With silver nitrate in excess the particles adsorb \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) instead, giving \(\mathrm{AgI}/\mathrm{Ag^+}\), a POSITIVELY charged sol. The charge is decided by which reagent is in excess, not by the substance.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Define transition metals. Why Zn, Cd and Hg are not called transition metals ? How is the variability in oxidation states of transition metals different from that of p-block elements ?
rows.solution:
A TRANSITION METAL is one whose atom, or one of whose stable ions, has a PARTLY FILLED d SUBSHELL.

The two conditions matter equally. Copper is \(3d^{10}\) as the ATOM, which would seem to exclude it, but \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is \(3d^9\) — partly filled — so copper IS a transition metal.

ZINC, CADMIUM AND MERCURY are excluded because they are \(d^{10}\) as atoms AND \(d^{10}\) as their \(+2\) ions, so neither condition is met. Everything that a partly filled d subshell brings is absent from them: their compounds are white and diamagnetic, they show only the \(+2\) state, they are poor catalysts, and their melting points are unusually low.

THE DIFFERENCE IN VARIABILITY: transition metals show oxidation states differing by ONE; p-block elements show states differing by TWO.

TRANSITION METALS — the \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) electrons lie close in energy and are removed ONE AT A TIME, so consecutive states appear. Manganese gives \(+2\), \(+3\), \(+4\), \(+6\) and \(+7\); iron gives \(+2\) and \(+3\).

P-BLOCK ELEMENTS — their variability comes from the INERT PAIR EFFECT, in which the outer \(s\) PAIR is either retained in full or lost in full. Tin gives \(+2\) and \(+4\), lead gives \(+2\) and \(+4\), and no \(+3\) state of either is seen.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
What happens when
(i) Propanone is treated with \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}\) and then hydrolysed ?
(ii) Ethanal is treated with excess ethanol and acid ?
(iii) Methanal undergoes Cannizzaro reaction ?
rows.solution:
(i) The Grignard reagent adds its methyl group to the carbonyl carbon, and hydrolysis gives the alcohol:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}OH}\)

The product is 2-METHYLPROPAN-2-OL, a TERTIARY alcohol — as a KETONE always gives, its carbonyl carbon already bearing two carbons and gaining a third.

(ii) With EXCESS ethanol and dry acid the aldehyde goes past the hemiacetal to the ACETAL:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{dry HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OC_2H_5)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is 1,1-DIETHOXYETHANE. Acetals are stable to base and to hydride but revert to the aldehyde with dilute acid, which is why they are used to PROTECT a carbonyl group.

(iii) Methanal has NO \(\alpha\) HYDROGEN, so with concentrated alkali it disproportionates — one molecule oxidised, another reduced:
\(2\,\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{NaOH\ (conc.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOONa}\)

The products are METHANOL and SODIUM FORMATE.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Write the main product in the following reactions :
(i) \(\mathrm{2CH_3COCl + (CH_3)_2Cd \rightarrow}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO \xrightarrow{\text{Zn (Hg) /Conc HCl}}}\)
(iii) \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}COONa + NaOH \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{CaO}}}\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - in sub-part (iii) the paper DRAWS the reactant's ring rather than naming it, and at 4x zoom that hexagon carries NO inner circle and NO double bonds, i.e. it is a CYCLOHEXANE ring, not benzene. The marking scheme confirms this: its answer for (iii) is Cyclohexane (drawn as a plain hexagon), which is only reachable from sodium cyclohexanecarboxylate. I have therefore READ the drawing losslessly into the stem as \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}COONa}\) rather than approximating it, and flag it REQUIRED so the crop is attached and the dedup guard fires - a sibling set drawing an aromatic ring here would produce a near-identical stem for a genuinely different question. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
(i) DIMETHYLCADMIUM is the mild reagent that stops an acyl chloride at the KETONE:
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3COCl} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} + \mathrm{CdCl_2}\)

The product is PROPANONE. A Grignard reagent would add twice and give 2-methylpropan-2-ol; the dialkylcadmium is reactive enough to attack the acyl chloride but not the ketone it produces.

(ii) Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid is the CLEMMENSEN REDUCTION, which takes the carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\):
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Zn(Hg)}/\text{conc. }\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3}\)

The product is PROPANE.

(iii) A sodium carboxylate heated with soda lime undergoes DECARBOXYLATION, losing carbon dioxide and giving the hydrocarbon with one carbon fewer:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}COONa} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{C_6H_{12}} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)

The product is CYCLOHEXANE. The calcium oxide keeps the alkali dry and stops it attacking the glass.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Amines
rows.stem:
Give reasons :
(i) Ammonolysis of alkyl halides is not a good method to prepare pure primary amines.
(ii) Aniline does not give Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(iii) Although \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group is o/p directing in electrophilic substitution reactions, yet aniline on nitration gives good yield of m-nitroaniline.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the reaction does not STOP at the primary amine.

Each product is a BETTER NUCLEOPHILE than the starting material, since every alkyl group added releases electron density onto the nitrogen. So the primary amine competes with ammonia for the next molecule of halide, and the secondary competes in turn:
\(\mathrm{NH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{RNH_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R_2NH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R_3N} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R_4N^+X^-}\)

The product is a mixture of all four, difficult to separate. Using a LARGE EXCESS of ammonia improves matters, since each halide molecule is then far more likely to meet ammonia than a product amine — but the GABRIEL synthesis, which cannot go past the first stage, is the proper method for a pure primary amine.

(ii) Because the amino group reacts with the CATALYST.

A Friedel-Crafts reaction needs anhydrous aluminium chloride, a LEWIS ACID, and aniline's nitrogen lone pair makes it a Lewis BASE — so the two combine at once to form a salt. The catalyst is consumed, and the nitrogen now carries a POSITIVE charge which strongly DEACTIVATES the ring, so no electrophilic substitution occurs.

(iii) Because nitration is carried out in a STRONGLY ACIDIC medium, in which aniline is largely PROTONATED.

The nitrating mixture converts aniline to the ANILINIUM ion, and \(-\overset{+}{\mathrm{N}}\mathrm{H_3}\) has no lone pair to donate and carries a positive charge, so it withdraws density powerfully and becomes META DIRECTING, like a nitro group.

The mixture therefore contains two species reacting in parallel: the little free aniline giving ortho and para products, and the protonated form giving meta. The result is about 47% meta, far more than a simple ortho, para director would give. Acetylation is used when a clean para product is wanted, since acetanilide is not basic enough to be protonated.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Which acid of the following pair would you expect to be stronger ?
\(\mathrm{F-CH_2-COOH}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\)
(ii) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their boiling points :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH,\ CH_3-CHO,\ CH_3-COOH}\)
(iii) Give simple chemical test to distinguish between Benzaldehyde and Acetophenone.
rows.solution:
(i) FLUOROACETIC ACID is the stronger.

Acid strength is decided by the stability of the anion left behind. FLUORINE is strongly electronegative and WITHDRAWS electron density through the \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect, spreading the carboxylate's negative charge and stabilising the anion. The METHYL group of acetic acid does the opposite, RELEASING density and intensifying the charge.

The \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) values record the gap: 2.59 against 4.76, a factor of about 150 in acid strength.

(ii) Increasing boiling point:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} < \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

All three are of comparable molar mass, so the order is set by the INTERMOLECULAR FORCES.

Ethanal has a polar carbonyl but no \(\mathrm{O-H}\), so only dipole-dipole attraction — 293 K. Ethanol has one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) and forms hydrogen bonds in an open chain — 351 K. Ethanoic acid forms TWO hydrogen bonds between each pair of molecules, locking them into a DIMER, and boils highest of all — 391 K.

(iii) Use TOLLENS' REAGENT. Warmed with it, BENZALDEHYDE gives a bright SILVER MIRROR, the aldehyde being oxidised while silver ion is reduced to the metal; ACETOPHENONE, a ketone, gives no reaction.

The IODOFORM test distinguishes them too, but in the OPPOSITE direction: acetophenone carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group and gives a yellow precipitate, while benzaldehyde does not.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Which will undergo faster nucleophilic addition reaction ?
Acetaldehyde or Propanone
(ii) What is the composition of Fehling's reagent ?
(iii) Draw structure of the semicarbazone of Ethanal.
rows.solution:
(i) ACETALDEHYDE undergoes the faster nucleophilic addition.

Addition begins with a nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon, so the reaction is faster the more POSITIVE and the more ACCESSIBLE that carbon is — and alkyl groups reduce both. Each one RELEASES electron density inductively, lowering the positive charge, and each one physically BLOCKS the approach.

Acetaldehyde carries ONE methyl group on its carbonyl carbon; propanone carries TWO. Both effects therefore run against propanone, twice over.

(ii) FEHLING'S REAGENT is made by mixing EQUAL VOLUMES of two solutions immediately before use.

FEHLING'S SOLUTION A is aqueous COPPER(II) SULPHATE.
FEHLING'S SOLUTION B is alkaline SODIUM POTASSIUM TARTRATE, Rochelle salt.

The tartrate is there to complex the copper(II) and keep it in solution; without it the alkali would simply precipitate copper(II) hydroxide. Warmed with an aldehyde, the deep blue mixture gives a RED precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

(iii) Semicarbazide condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water, and only its TERMINAL \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) attacks — the other nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised into the carbonyl and is not nucleophilic:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH{=}N{-}NH{-}CO{-}NH_2}\)

That is ETHANAL SEMICARBAZONE.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: What is the effect of temperature on the rate constant of a reaction ?
rows.context:
The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. A number of factors such as temperature, concentration of reactants, catalyst affect the rate of reaction. Mathematical representation of rate of a reaction is given by rate law :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[A]^{x}\,[B]^{y}}\)
x and y indicate how sensitive the rate is to the change in concentration of A and B. Sum of x + y gives the overall order of a reaction.
When a sequence of elementary reactions gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions. Molecularity and order of an elementary reaction are same. Zero order reactions are relatively uncommon but they occur under special conditions. All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.
rows.solution:
The rate constant INCREASES with temperature.

The Arrhenius equation gives \(k = \mathrm{A}e^{-E_a/\mathrm{RT}}\). Raising \(\mathrm{T}\) makes the exponent less negative, so the exponential term grows and \(k\) with it.

The physical reason is not that the molecules collide more often — that effect is small — but that a far larger FRACTION of the collisions now carry at least the activation energy. Near room temperature a rise of ten degrees roughly DOUBLES the rate constant for a typical reaction.

Note what does NOT change: the ACTIVATION ENERGY itself is fixed by the nature of the reactants, and only a catalyst alters it.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: For a reaction A + B \(\rightarrow\) Product, the rate law is given by, Rate = \(\mathrm{k[A]^{2}\,[B]^{1/2}}\). What is the order of the reaction ?
rows.context:
The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. A number of factors such as temperature, concentration of reactants, catalyst affect the rate of reaction. Mathematical representation of rate of a reaction is given by rate law :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[A]^{x}\,[B]^{y}}\)
x and y indicate how sensitive the rate is to the change in concentration of A and B. Sum of x + y gives the overall order of a reaction.
When a sequence of elementary reactions gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions. Molecularity and order of an elementary reaction are same. Zero order reactions are relatively uncommon but they occur under special conditions. All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.
rows.solution:
The ORDER is the sum of the exponents in the rate law:
\(\text{Order} = 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} = 2{\cdot}5\)

A FRACTIONAL order is perfectly possible, and it is worth noticing what it tells us. Order is a MEASURED quantity, read off experiment, so it need not be a whole number and need not match the coefficients in the balanced equation — which here would have predicted 1 and 1.

A fractional order is in fact evidence that the reaction is COMPLEX, going through a sequence of steps rather than a single collision. MOLECULARITY, by contrast, counts colliding species and must be a whole number of at least 1.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: How order and molecularity are different for complex reactions ?
rows.context:
The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. A number of factors such as temperature, concentration of reactants, catalyst affect the rate of reaction. Mathematical representation of rate of a reaction is given by rate law :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[A]^{x}\,[B]^{y}}\)
x and y indicate how sensitive the rate is to the change in concentration of A and B. Sum of x + y gives the overall order of a reaction.
When a sequence of elementary reactions gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions. Molecularity and order of an elementary reaction are same. Zero order reactions are relatively uncommon but they occur under special conditions. All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.
rows.solution:
For a COMPLEX reaction the two part company completely: ORDER can be determined, MOLECULARITY cannot.

ORDER is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity, read off the measured rate law. It applies to the reaction as a whole, is governed by the SLOWEST step, and may be zero, fractional or negative.

MOLECULARITY is a THEORETICAL quantity, counting the species that must COLLIDE SIMULTANEOUSLY in a SINGLE elementary step. It must be a whole number of at least 1, and rarely exceeds 3.

A complex reaction is a SEQUENCE of elementary steps, each possibly with its own molecularity, so the sequence as a whole has none to quote — there is no one collision to count. The two coincide only for an ELEMENTARY reaction, where the single step IS the reaction.

rows.subtopic: Integrated Rate Equations
rows.stem: A first order reaction has a rate constant \(2 \times 10^{-3}\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). How long will 6g of this reactant take to reduce to 2g ?
rows.context:
The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. A number of factors such as temperature, concentration of reactants, catalyst affect the rate of reaction. Mathematical representation of rate of a reaction is given by rate law :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[A]^{x}\,[B]^{y}}\)
x and y indicate how sensitive the rate is to the change in concentration of A and B. Sum of x + y gives the overall order of a reaction.
When a sequence of elementary reactions gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions. Molecularity and order of an elementary reaction are same. Zero order reactions are relatively uncommon but they occur under special conditions. All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.
rows.solution:
The reaction is FIRST ORDER, so the integrated rate law can be used with MASSES directly — the units cancel in the ratio:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Rearranging for the time, with 6 g falling to 2 g:
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\log\dfrac{6}{2} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{2 \times 10^{-3}} \times \log 3\)
\(= 1151{\cdot}5 \times 0{\cdot}4771\)

\(t = 549{\cdot}38\ \mathrm{s}\), a little over nine minutes

A rough check: the half-life is \(0{\cdot}693/(2 \times 10^{-3}) = 346{\cdot}5\) s, and falling to a THIRD takes rather more than one half-life but less than two — 549 s sits correctly between 346 and 693.

rows.subtopic: Integrated Rate Equations
rows.stem:
The half life for radioactive decay of \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) is 6930 years. An archaeological artifact containing wood had only 75% of the \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) found in a living tree. Find the age of the sample.
[log 4 = 0.6021   log 3 = 0.4771   log 2 = 0.3010   log 10 = 1]
rows.context:
The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. A number of factors such as temperature, concentration of reactants, catalyst affect the rate of reaction. Mathematical representation of rate of a reaction is given by rate law :
\(\mathrm{Rate = k[A]^{x}\,[B]^{y}}\)
x and y indicate how sensitive the rate is to the change in concentration of A and B. Sum of x + y gives the overall order of a reaction.
When a sequence of elementary reactions gives us the products, the reactions are called complex reactions. Molecularity and order of an elementary reaction are same. Zero order reactions are relatively uncommon but they occur under special conditions. All natural and artificial radioactive decay of unstable nuclei take place by first order kinetics.
rows.solution:
Radioactive decay is FIRST ORDER, so start from the half-life:
\(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{6930} = 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{year^{-1}}\)

The artifact retains 75% of the carbon-14 of a living tree, so taking the original as 100 the amount left is 75:
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{75} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{10^{-4}}\log\dfrac{4}{3}\)

Using the logarithms supplied, \(\log 4 - \log 3 = 0{\cdot}6021 - 0{\cdot}4771 = 0{\cdot}125\):
\(t = 23030 \times 0{\cdot}125\)

\(t = 2878{\cdot}75\ \mathrm{years}\)

The figure is reasonable on its face: losing only a quarter of the carbon-14 must take substantially LESS than one half-life of 6930 years, and 2879 years is comfortably under half of it.

This is the principle of RADIOCARBON DATING. A living organism keeps its carbon-14 topped up by exchange with the atmosphere; once it dies the exchange stops and the isotope decays at a known rate, so what remains measures the time since death.
